final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. Yes. The husband's best recourse runs through the immigration court first. File a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order based on lack of notice, then use the reopened case to pursue the I-130/I-485. No filing fee is due for that motion.

1. Immigration court filing (as of April 1, 2026). File one motion to reopen to rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia order with the immigration court that entered it (the Immigration Judge). Authority: INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), and 8 C.F.R. 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). An order entered in absentia may be rescinded on a motion filed at any time if the noncitizen shows he did not receive notice in accordance with INA 239(a)(1) or (2). The 180-day deadline that applies to 'exceptional circumstances' motions does not apply. Only one such motion is allowed. Filing it automatically stays removal pending the IJ's decision. Practical points: (a) File promptly and, if possible, via the court's electronic system (ECAS) or by mail, with proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA. Include a cover page marked 'Motion to Reopen - In Absentia - Automatic Stay', a proposed order, and a sworn declaration from the husband (and wife) explaining the address problem. (b) File a Form EOIR-33 change of address, which should be filed with or before the motion. (c) Attach evidence that the NTA and any hearing notice went to an address the husband never gave: the I-130/I-485 filings and receipt notices showing the correct address, the RFE/denial envelopes or USCIS records, and any FOIA or EOIR records (the NTA, hearing notice, and certificate of service). (d) Request rescission, termination or a fresh hearing, and state that he intends to pursue relief (adjustment of status) so the IJ has a basis for the next step. Also consider requesting a stay of removal in the alternative (Form EOIR-? not required; the stay is automatic).

Substantive standard. The key question is whether he got proper notice. For an in absentia order, the government must show written notice under INA 239(a)(1) (NTA) or 239(a)(2) (notice of change in time/place), and notice by mail is effective only if sent to the address the noncitizen provided under 239(a)(1)(F) or to his last known address. Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), holds that a notice of hearing under 239(a)(2) alone can defeat a notice-based challenge even if the NTA was defective, so the motion should show that no NTA and no hearing notice reached him through a proper address. Because the NTA was mailed to a wrong address he never gave (and which USCIS also used), there is a strong argument that notice was not 'in accordance with' 239(a)(1) or (2) and that 239(a)(1)(F) address-duty presumptions do not apply. Caveat: courts differ on how much the husband's own address obligations and the 'last known address' concept matter, and circuit law matters; the filing location's circuit should be checked. I did not verify the circuit-specific law.

2. Fees. There is no fee. Under H.R. 1 (2025), EOIR's new $900 motion-to-reopen fee has an express exception for a motion to reopen an in absentia order filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) on the notice ground. (Practice sources also state no fee for such motions.) If the motion instead rests on 'exceptional circumstances,' the fee would apply ($900 unless waived). Also note: if the case is reopened and he later files an I-485 with the court, or the I-130 is appealed, separate H.R. 1/EOIR and USCIS fees may apply; I did not verify those amounts. A fee waiver request is possible for fee-bearing filings.

3. Contesting the I-130 and I-485 denials. (a) The USCIS denials. The I-130 was denied as abandoned for not responding to the RFE (8 C.F.R. 103.2(b)(8)(iv)-(13)). A denial for abandonment cannot be appealed but can be challenged by a motion to reopen under 8 C.F.R. 103.5 (Form I-290B), including on the ground that the RFE was sent to the wrong address. The normal deadline is 30 days (33 by mail), long expired (December 2023/January 2024). 8 C.F.R. 103.5(a)(1)(i) allows USCIS discretion to excuse delay for a motion to reopen if the delay was reasonable and beyond the applicant's control, which fits non-receipt by USCIS error; the I-290B filing fee should be checked. Note also that USCIS's I-485 denial was likely a consequence of the I-130 denial, so reopening the I-130 is the key. Alternatively, file a new I-130 (and I-485) with the wife as petitioner. (b) Adjustment in removal proceedings. Once the order is rescinded and proceedings are reopened, the IJ has exclusive jurisdiction over a renewed I-485 for a person in proceedings (8 C.F.R. 1245.2(a)(1)); the IJ may review an I-485 de novo, and the I-130 can be pending or approved with USCIS (or the IJ can continue the case for USCIS adjudication). Because he entered on a B-2 visa, was inspected and admitted, and is an immediate relative, he can adjust under INA 245(a) and the 245(c) bars generally do not apply to immediate relatives. (c) Risk: marriage 19 days after entry on a B-2 visa raises a preconceived-intent / willful misrepresentation concern (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i); State Dept. '90-day rule' as persuasive guidance), which USCIS or the IJ may probe, and the bona fides of the marriage will be tested. (d) Federal court review is limited; mandamus/APA review of the denials is unlikely to help given 8 U.S.C. 1252(a)(2)(B) and the availability of administrative remedies.

4. Alternatives. If the notice argument fails, consider a motion to reopen sua sponte, or exceptional-circumstances reopening (not available after 180 days), and a petition for review of the IJ's denial to the court of appeals within 30 days. Also, voluntary departure/ removal consequences: he should avoid leaving the US, as departure after an order could trigger INA 212(a)(9)(A) and (B) bars and execution of the order. Because ICE can execute the in absentia order until stayed, he should file the motion immediately; the automatic stay protects him once filed.

Caveat: I could not retrieve the primary text of the statute or regulations directly (several sites were blocked), so quotations are drawn from secondary summaries; confirm against the current eCFR/U.S. Code and current EOIR fee guidance before filing.
